paragraphs.text: In competitive rock climbing, scaling the sheer granite face of El Cuervo in under ten minutes was called “splitting the vertical mile.” Although such a pace up a wall of that height was considered humanly impossible, several elite climbers aimed to break that supposedly impenetrable barrier. One of them was a twenty-three-year-old engineering student named Imogen Castellan.

Castellan had tasted failure at the regional championship two years earlier. There, she was favored to win the speed-climbing final, but she finished in a disappointing fifth place instead. Castellan's performance was a letdown for her and her club, Ridgeline. Determined to redeem herself, Castellan postponed her plans to step back from competition and focused on the ultimate prize—breaking the ten-minute barrier on El Cuervo.

Castellan attacked the elusive milestone with discipline and careful planning. The climber decided to use intensive interval training to build endurance and precision. For these workouts, Castellan climbed the same forty-foot practice pitch twelve times in a row, aiming for eighteen seconds each climb. Between intervals, she let her forearms recover for ninety seconds.

By early spring, Castellan had succeeded in lowering her pitch time to nineteen seconds, but she had to shave off at least one more second to reach her target. Frustrated by the plateau she had reached, Castellan took a break from training and spent four days kayaking on a nearby river. The rest from climbing let her shoulders recuperate and left her feeling refreshed. When Castellan returned to the practice wall, she completed twelve pitches at seventeen seconds each. She finally felt prepared to attempt the record.

As a member of the Ridgeline Climbing Club, Castellan entered an exhibition event at El Cuervo against a visiting university team. The event took place on the granite face on April 12. Castellan and her two Ridgeline teammates, Sana Okafor and Teo Alvarez, were close friends and frequent training partners. Okafor and Alvarez agreed to help Castellan accomplish her goal by serving as her “markers.”

In speed climbing, markers are climbers who scale a nearby route at a planned, steady pace so a teammate can glance over and judge her own rhythm without stopping to check a stopwatch. Climbing beside a marker, a competitor can sense pace almost automatically, and by matching a marker's rhythm, a climber conserves energy she might otherwise waste second-guessing herself. When the start horn sounded, Alvarez pulled ahead on the adjacent route, and Castellan matched his pace beside him.

Caught up in the excitement, Castellan lost her instinctive feel for her pace and called out “Faster!” to Alvarez. Alvarez, however, stayed composed and held his current steady but grueling rhythm, clearing the first third of the wall in one minute fifty seconds. Then Okafor surged ahead on the adjacent route, matching Castellan's pace for the middle third. At the base of the final overhang, Castellan pulled past Okafor. Castellan said, “I knew the moment had finally come. There was no fear left, only motion and purpose.” Castellan touched the summit anchor in 9 minutes 58 seconds. The crowd below erupted the instant the timer flashed a number that began with nine.

Soon after Castellan's achievement, three other climbers matched her pace. A new mindset had taken root among speed climbers. Over the years, the record continued to fall. However, the current record, 8 minutes 41 seconds, has stood unbroken since 2019. Some question whether this record represents the limits of human ability. But perhaps there is another Castellan, a climber who, with patience and nerve, will accomplish the next impossible thing.

questions.question: The words “feat,” “humanly impossible,” and “impenetrable barrier” in paragraph 1 affect the tone of the paragraph because they

options.A: highlight the idea that only the most skilled climbers would be able to climb El Cuervo quickly.
options.B: emphasize the idea that climbing El Cuervo in under ten minutes was a seemingly unattainable goal.
options.C: convey the competitiveness among elite climbers to consistently set and break speed records.
options.D: show the intensity of the training programs climbers endure in order to achieve their goals.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. These words suggest the feat was unattainable even for the most skilled climbers, which overstates the point. B. CORRECT. No one had ever split the vertical mile; “humanly impossible” and “impenetrable barrier” imply the goal seemed unattainable. C. Incorrect. The paragraph focuses on Castellan specifically, not competitiveness among elite climbers in general. D. Incorrect. The training program is described in paragraphs 3-4; these words relate to the magnitude of the goal itself, not the intensity of training.

questions.question: Read these sentences from paragraph 7. “Castellan said, ‘I knew the moment had finally come. There was no fear left, only motion and purpose.’” The sentences contribute to the development of ideas in the passage by showing that Castellan

options.A: knew that she was about to achieve the goal she had worked toward.
options.B: was no longer experiencing personal disappointment from her past failure at the regional championship.
options.C: felt grateful to her teammates for helping her take the lead.
options.D: was satisfied that her training had helped her perfect her climbing technique.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Castellan's sense that “the moment had finally come” and the feeling of having “motion and purpose” reveal her awareness that she was on the verge of achieving her long-sought goal. B, C, D. Incorrect — the lines focus on Castellan's realization that her goal was within reach, not on resolving past disappointment, gratitude toward teammates, or technique.

questions.question: Which sentence best supports the idea that Castellan needed an alternative to “careful planning” (paragraph 3) in order to accomplish her goal?

options.A: “Castellan's performance was a letdown for her and her club, Ridgeline.” (paragraph 2)
options.B: “The climber decided to use intensive interval training to build endurance and precision.” (paragraph 3)
options.C: “For these workouts, Castellan climbed the same forty-foot practice pitch twelve times in a row, aiming for eighteen seconds each climb.” (paragraph 3)
options.D: “Frustrated by the plateau she had reached, Castellan took a break from training and spent four days kayaking on a nearby river.” (paragraph 4)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the championship loss prompted a new goal, not an alternative training method. B. Incorrect — describes her training plan itself, not an alternative to it. C. Incorrect — details of the interval training plan, not an alternative form of preparation. D. CORRECT — explains Castellan reached a point where she couldn't improve despite her strict plan; the kayaking break “let her shoulders recuperate and left her feeling refreshed” (paragraph 4) — this is the alternative to careful planning.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage indicates that Castellan nearly made a mistake that would have cost her the record?

options.A: “By early spring, Castellan had succeeded in lowering her pitch time to nineteen seconds, but she had to shave off at least one more second to reach her target.” (paragraph 4)
options.B: “When the start horn sounded, Alvarez pulled ahead on the adjacent route, and Castellan matched his pace beside him.” (paragraph 6)
options.C: “Caught up in the excitement, Castellan lost her instinctive feel for her pace and called out ‘Faster!’ to Alvarez.” (paragraph 7)
options.D: “At the base of the final overhang, Castellan pulled past Okafor.” (paragraph 7)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — describes a training challenge, not a race mistake. B. Incorrect — describes the start of the climb going to plan. C. CORRECT — if Castellan had climbed faster than her marker's pace she could have burned out before the overhang; losing her “instinctive feel for her pace” in excitement was a near mistake. D. Incorrect — describes Castellan moving ahead of the second marker at the appropriate, planned point, not a mistake.

questions.question: Castellan's loss at the regional championship influenced her decision to pursue splitting the vertical mile by

options.A: allowing her to recognize her weaknesses and improve her climbing ability.
options.B: prompting her to take a different approach to her regular training.
options.C: motivating her to prove to herself that she could set and achieve a goal.
options.D: giving her the opportunity to reach a goal no climber had ever accomplished.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the loss made her “determined to redeem herself” and focus specifically on the ten-minute wall, not just general improvement. B. Incorrect — the different training approach came later (the spring plateau), not directly from the championship loss. C. CORRECT — she sought redemption after her “disappointing fifth place,” responding by setting a goal to conquer the “ultimate prize.” D. Incorrect — the loss motivated a change in focus, not an “opportunity” itself.

paragraphs.text: It was at that time the policy of the trustees and officers of the Hawthorne Institute neither to employ collectors nor to send out expeditions in search of specimens. The institute decided to depend upon voluntary contributions, and I was always busy, part of the day, in drafting replies to correspondents who wrote offering their services as trappers, collectors of all sorts of fauna, and also to those who offered specimens for sale, usually at exorbitant rates.

To the proprietors of . . . molting parrots, lame foxes, and sun-bleached turtle shells I returned courteous but uncompromising refusals—of course, first submitting all such letters, together with my replies, to Dr. Abernathy Voss.

One afternoon toward the end of May, however, just as I was leaving the storage annex to return to my desk, a junior archivist called out to me that Dr. Voss wanted to see me a moment; so I retraced my steps to the curator's office. The doctor, who was sitting at his desk before a pile of letters and replies submitted for my approval, pushed his glasses down and looked over them at me with a thin smile that suggested amusement, impatience, and perhaps a faint trace of apology.
“Now, here's a letter,” he said, with a deliberate gesture toward a sheet of paper impaled on a file—“a letter that I suppose you remember.” He disengaged the sheet of paper and handed it to me.
“Oh yes,” I replied, with a shrug; “of course the man is mistaken—or—”
“Or what?” demanded Dr. Voss, tranquilly, wiping his glasses.
“—Or a liar,” I replied.

After a silence he leaned back in his chair and bade me read the letter to him again, and I did so with a contemptuous tolerance for the writer, who must have been either a very innocent victim or a very stubborn fraud. I said as much to Dr. Voss, but, to my surprise, he appeared to waver.
“I suppose,” he said, with his near-sighted, embarrassed smile, “that nine hundred and ninety-nine men in a thousand would throw that letter aside and condemn the writer as a liar or a fool?”
“In my opinion,” said I, “he's one or the other.”
“He isn't—in mine,” said the doctor, placidly.
“What!” I exclaimed. “Here is a man living alone at a lighthouse at the edge of the world, who wants you to send somebody to take charge of a bird that doesn't exist!”
“How do you know,” asked Dr. Voss, “that the bird in question does not exist?”

“It is generally accepted,” I replied, sarcastically, “that the Eskimo curlew has been extinct for decades. Therefore I may be pardoned for doubting that our correspondent possesses a pair of them alive.”
“Oh, you young fellows,” said the doctor, smiling wearily, “you embark on theories for destinations that don't exist.”
He leaned back in his chair, his amused eyes searching space for the imagery that made him smile.
“Like kites in a gale, you chase a direction with real conviction, but you rarely land where you meant to—do you?”
Rather red in the face, I said: “Don't you believe the curlew to be extinct?”
“A reputable ornithologist photographed one in 1963.”
“Who has seen a single specimen since?”
“Nobody—except our correspondent here,” he replied, laughing.
I laughed, too, considering the interview at an end, but the doctor went on, coolly:
“Whatever it is that our correspondent has—and I am daring to believe that it is the curlew itself—I want you to secure it for the institute.”
When my astonishment subsided my first conscious sentiment was one of pity. Clearly, Dr. Voss was on the verge of dotage—ah, what a loss to the field!

I believe now that Dr. Voss perfectly interpreted my thoughts, but he betrayed neither resentment nor impatience. I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool's errand was none of my conceiving.
Together we made out a list of articles necessary for me and itemized the expenses I might incur, and I set a date for my return, allowing no margin for a successful termination to the expedition.
“Never mind that,” said the doctor. “What I want you to do is to get those birds here safely. Now, how many men will you take?”
“None,” I replied, bluntly; “it's a useless expense, unless there is something to bring back. If there is I'll wire you, you may be sure.”
“Very well,” said Dr. Voss, good-humoredly, “you shall have all the assistance you may require. Can you leave tonight?”
The old man was certainly prompt. I nodded, half-sulkily, aware of his amusement.

“So,” I said, picking up my coat, “I am to start north to find a lighthouse called Gray Point, where there is a man named Pruitt who possesses, among other household items, two extinct Eskimo curlews—”
We were both laughing by this time. I asked him why on earth he credited the assertion of a man he had never before heard of.

“I suppose,” he replied, with the same half-apologetic, half-humorous smile, “it is instinct. I feel, somehow, that this man Pruitt has got a curlew—perhaps two. I can't get away from the idea that we are on the eve of acquiring one of the rarest living creatures. It's odd for a scientist to talk as I do; doubtless you're shocked—admit it, now!”
But I was not shocked; on the contrary, I was conscious that the same strange hope that Dr. Voss cherished was beginning, in spite of me, to stir my pulse, too.
“If he has—” I began, then stopped.
The doctor and I looked hard at each other in silence.
“Go on,” he said, encouragingly.

But I had nothing more to say, for the prospect of beholding with my own eyes a living specimen of the Eskimo curlew produced a series of conflicting emotions within me which rendered speech entirely unnecessary.

questions.question: Read paragraph 2 from the excerpt. “To the proprietors of . . . molting parrots, lame foxes, and sun-bleached turtle shells I returned courteous but uncompromising refusals—of course, first submitting all such letters, together with my replies, to Dr. Abernathy Voss.” This paragraph helps develop the plot by establishing that the narrator

options.A: dislikes writing refusal letters for the specimens offered to the institute.
options.B: attempts to predict what Dr. Voss would say in the refusal letters.
options.C: believes that many of the specimens offered are not acceptable for the institute.
options.D: resents Dr. Voss's insistence on reviewing the refusal letters.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator shows no indication of disliking the work; the letters inform people whether the institute will accept the specimens. B. Incorrect. The narrator is confident in his own reply and doesn't anticipate differing from Dr. Voss. C. CORRECT. “Uncompromising refusals” indicates the narrator's initial confidence that the specimens in the letters aren't of value; this confidence is later shaken as the plot unfolds when Dr. Voss states “I am daring to believe that it is the curlew itself” (paragraph 23); the narrator's transition from dismissive doubt to budding hopefulness is a major part of the plot (paragraph 34). D. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't resent the review; “of course” in paragraph 2 shows he expects to submit letters to Dr. Voss as part of his job.

questions.question: Read this sentence from paragraph 3. “The doctor, who was sitting at his desk before a pile of letters and replies submitted for my approval, pushed his glasses down and looked over them at me with a thin smile that suggested amusement, impatience, and perhaps a faint trace of apology.” What does the phrase “a faint trace of apology” convey about Dr. Voss?

options.A: It indicates that Dr. Voss feels bad that he has to call the narrator to his office during work hours.
options.B: It shows that Dr. Voss is hesitant to share his opinions with the narrator.
options.C: It implies that Dr. Voss is uncomfortable criticizing the narrator's work.
options.D: It suggests that Dr. Voss knows that the conversation will be frustrating for the narrator.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The apologetic manner isn't about calling the narrator in; it's caused by Dr. Voss's understanding that the conversation about the letter/expedition will cause an argument; in paragraph 29 he asks if the narrator can leave that evening, showing he doesn't feel bad about taking the narrator's time. B. Incorrect. The paragraphs that follow show Dr. Voss sharing opinions without pause even when unflattering (paragraph 17). C. Incorrect. Dr. Voss is not uncomfortable challenging the narrator; he seems at ease. D. CORRECT. Dr. Voss is amused and annoyed by the narrator's dismissal of the possibility that curlews exist, and he knows the narrator will react negatively to being sent on what the narrator considers a “fool's errand” (paragraph 25).

questions.question: How does the exchange between Dr. Voss and the narrator in paragraphs 8-11 contribute to the development of the characters?

options.A: It establishes the conflict between Dr. Voss and the narrator concerning the validity of the letter.
options.B: It suggests a theme of collaboration because the narrator and Dr. Voss regularly work together.
options.C: It reveals the characters' traits by contrasting the narrator's distrust with how easily Dr. Voss is deceived by what he reads.
options.D: It hints that the resolution will involve the narrator accepting Dr. Voss's opinion about the content of the letter.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. It reveals the difference in opinions: the narrator believes without doubt that Pruitt (the letter writer about the curlews) is “a liar or a fool” (paragraph 9), while Dr. Voss believes the letter writer could be telling the truth (paragraph 8). B. Incorrect. The narrator reacts with “contemptuous tolerance” and is shocked Dr. Voss agrees with Pruitt (paragraph 11)—this is emphatic disagreement, not collaboration. C. Incorrect. Dr. Voss is portrayed as experienced and intelligent, not easily deceived. D. Incorrect. Paragraphs 8-11 primarily establish a difference of opinion, not a hint at the resolution.

questions.question: Dr. Voss's observations in paragraphs 15-17 create tension in the excerpt by causing the narrator to feel

options.A: flustered by Dr. Voss's criticism of his logic.
options.B: annoyed by Dr. Voss's sarcasm about his inexperience.
options.C: confused by Dr. Voss's lack of respect for his opinion.
options.D: frustrated by Dr. Voss's lack of interest in his theory.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Dr. Voss criticizes “you young fellows” (paragraph 15), suggesting the ideas of young scientists like the narrator are unsupported (“like kites in a gale” [paragraph 17]) and inaccurate (“you rarely land where you meant to—do you?” [paragraph 17]). The narrator becomes “rather red in the face” (paragraph 18), indicating he's upset, and asks Dr. Voss about the curlew in an attempt to defend himself. B. Incorrect. The narrator has a negative reaction, but Dr. Voss is genuine, not sarcastic; sarcasm comes from the narrator in paragraph 14. C. Incorrect. The narrator blushes with embarrassment, but understands Dr. Voss's point about his unquestioning acceptance that curlews don't exist. D. Incorrect. Dr. Voss shows amusement with the narrator's perspective, not disinterest.

questions.question: How does the interaction between the narrator and Dr. Voss in paragraphs 26-28 contribute to the development of the theme?

options.A: It illustrates Dr. Voss's patience as the narrator argues against making the expedition.
options.B: It reveals the narrator's frustration with his limited role in making decisions for the institute.
options.C: It emphasizes Dr. Voss's desire to acquire new specimens for the institute at any cost.
options.D: It shows the narrator's acceptance of his assignment despite his personal objections.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't argue against making the expedition; he argues that extra men are unnecessary (paragraph 28). B. Incorrect. The narrator's frustration comes from Dr. Voss criticizing his blind disbelief, not from an inability to make decisions. C. Incorrect. Dr. Voss states “what I want you to do is to get those birds here safely” (paragraph 27), prioritizing the birds' safety, not acquisition at any cost. D. CORRECT. Paragraph 26 describes practical planning despite the narrator “allowing no margin for a successful termination”; paragraph 28 shows his personal objections (he believes extra men are pointless) since he doesn't expect to find any curlews.

questions.question: Which sentence from the excerpt best explains why Dr. Voss is eager to send the narrator on an expedition?

options.A: “I believe now that Dr. Voss perfectly interpreted my thoughts, but he betrayed neither resentment nor impatience.” (paragraph 25)
options.B: “Together we made out a list of articles necessary for me and itemized the expenses I might incur, and I set a date for my return, allowing no margin for a successful termination to the expedition.” (paragraph 26)
options.C: “‘What I want you to do is to get those birds here safely.’” (paragraph 27)
options.D: “‘I can't get away from the idea that we are on the eve of acquiring one of the rarest living creatures.’” (paragraph 33)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The narrator suspects Dr. Voss is losing his ability to reason; this doesn't explain WHY Dr. Voss is excited. B. Incorrect. Shows planning logistics, not the underlying reason for his eagerness. C. Incorrect. Shows interest in the birds' safety but not the underlying reason (rarity). D. CORRECT. Reveals Dr. Voss's excitement to get “one of the rarest living creatures,” the curlew. In paragraph 14 the narrator states the curlew is “generally accepted” as extinct, making a living specimen incredibly rare and explaining Dr. Voss's eagerness.

questions.question: How does paragraph 34 help develop the plot of the excerpt?

options.A: It shows that the narrator is beginning to consider the possibility of finding the curlews.
options.B: It demonstrates that the narrator is struggling to understand why Dr. Voss thinks the curlews exist.
options.C: It establishes that the narrator is willing to let Dr. Voss overrule him about the curlews.
options.D: It emphasizes that the narrator feels a sense of urgency to complete the expedition to locate the curlews.

solution.exhibit_text: A. CORRECT. Despite initial disbelief, the narrator admits in paragraph 34 that he's starting to feel the “same strange hope” Dr. Voss feels (paragraph 33). B. Incorrect. Paragraph 34 reveals the narrator is affected by the “strange hope,” beginning to share it “in spite of” himself—not struggling to understand. C. Incorrect. The hope described wouldn't be present if the narrator were simply overruled without sharing the belief; his willingness to be overruled was already established in paragraph 25. D. Incorrect. The narrator doesn't express urgency in paragraph 34; he expresses hope that the curlews might really exist.

questions.question: Which sentence best demonstrates the professional relationship between the narrator and Dr. Voss?

options.A: “He disengaged the sheet of paper and handed it to me.” (paragraph 4)
options.B: “Clearly, Dr. Voss was on the verge of dotage—ah, what a loss to the field!” (paragraph 24)
options.C: “I drew a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but to obey, and this fool's errand was none of my conceiving.” (paragraph 25)
options.D: “‘Very well,’ said Dr. Voss, good-humoredly, ‘you shall have all the assistance you may require.’” (paragraph 29)

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. This doesn't convey a subordinate/superior relationship. B. Incorrect. This is a momentary reaction, not a demonstration of the professional relationship. C. CORRECT. The narrator disagrees (“this fool's errand was none of my conceiving”) but obeys because he works for Dr. Voss (“there was nothing to do but to obey”). D. Incorrect. Dr. Voss's good-humored offer doesn't best demonstrate the underlying employer-employee relationship.

questions.question: How does the author develop the contrast between the narrator's point of view and Dr. Voss's point of view?

options.A: by providing both the narrator's and Dr. Voss's thoughts on how age and experience influence each other's reasoning
options.B: by using the conversation between the narrator and Dr. Voss to emphasize their reactions to the letter
options.C: by describing Dr. Voss's persistent efforts to change the narrator's mind about the letter
options.D: by including dialogue that explains why Dr. Voss is the supervisor and the narrator is his subordinate

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect. The excerpt doesn't describe the narrator's thoughts on age/experience in enough detail. B. CORRECT. The primary conflict revolves around the narrator's disagreement with Dr. Voss about whether the letter about the curlews could be true; the narrator dismisses the possibility out of hand (paragraphs 5, 12), while Dr. Voss calmly admits most people would dismiss the letter (paragraph 9) yet himself believes the writer could be telling the truth (paragraph 13). C. Incorrect. Dr. Voss explains the disagreement (paragraphs 19-21) but doesn't make persistent efforts to convince the narrator; instead, he states the narrator will go on the expedition regardless. D. Incorrect. The dialogue's point isn't to explain the subordinate-supervisor relationship, but to contrast what each character believes about the letter's contents.

ela_passages.title: Counting the Grains of the Night Sky

lines.text: There are the things the night sky is made of,
lights we can see and name, and then
there are the things even older, things that seem
to reach us only after they are gone.
So beyond the stars we can count are galaxies,
and beyond the galaxies, we find
clusters, filaments, the edges of everything; and beyond that—
what, exactly? Because we are asking about
everything here: your porch light,
the moon over the parking lot,
the sun your grandmother squints against,
the comet your little brother missed,
and the telescope he begs to borrow every August.
And everywhere.
Everything and everywhere
are lit by the same old fire, whatever
it is. How do we find it? We can listen for it
in the static from deep space,
murmuring back to us from unimaginable
distances. Or we can build long,
wide silver dishes across the desert
and aim them at particular patches of dark
(like casting nets, only very patient nets
strung out for decades at a time)
until everything we think we've mapped
brushes against everything we haven't.
And there, in the sudden flare, in the static,
blazing briefly, they appear:
the quasars, the pulsars, and the blazars;
the magnetars and the supernovae. Their names
sound like villains or maybe spells
muttered by someone in an old arcade.
The one thing we know for sure
is that they burn. This is how starlight
enters our world, how our nights are held
both bright and dark, what keeps
the tide pulled toward the shore tonight
as well as pointed away from, say,
the moon above it. They burn, and it is only out there
in the static—in the vast dark
where astronomers write down
what they can, whatever seems most real—
that they let us notice their slow burning,
answering to the dark they come from.

questions.question: Read lines 5-8 from the poem. The lines help develop a central idea of the poem by revealing the speaker's

options.A: interest in determining how the parts of the universe work together.
options.B: curiosity about what makes up the structure of the universe.
options.C: desire to prove that galaxies make up the universe.
options.D: questions about what tools are needed to study the universe.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — lines 5-8 demonstrate knowledge about the structure of the universe, not interest in how parts work together. B. CORRECT — lines 5-8 show connection using “beyond” repeatedly; the progression from stars to galaxies to clusters ends with the question “what, exactly?” (line 8), showing the speaker's curiosity about mysteries still unsolved about the structure of the universe — a central idea. C. Incorrect — the speaker expresses curiosity, not a desire to prove a point; no conflict is shown. D. Incorrect — the poem later discusses telescopes and dishes (tools), but lines 5-8 specifically are about structures themselves, not tools.

questions.question: The main purpose of the comparison in lines 23-24 of the poem is to show

options.A: that the signals' faintness makes them difficult to detect.
options.B: how the dishes search for signals over time.
options.C: that the signals have a familiar shape.
options.D: how the signals can be detected only in darkness.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the comparison focuses on the searching process, not detectability. B. CORRECT — lines 23-24 describe “very patient nets / strung out for decades at a time,” describing how the dishes search patiently over long stretches of time. C. Incorrect — the lines describe a process, not a shape. D. Incorrect — “strung out” refers to duration, not darkness.

questions.question: Read lines 28-29 from the poem. The imagery in the lines reveals that the speaker

options.A: envies the astronomers who research distant signals.
options.B: has personally observed a quasar or pulsar.
options.C: admires the dramatic flare that occurs when a signal is detected.
options.D: has a simplistic understanding of how signals are detected.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the astronomers in the final stanza are observers; the speaker in lines 28-29 is focused on the signal itself, not the astronomers. B. Incorrect — the speaker's understanding is based on astronomers' observations, not personal witness. C. CORRECT — “sudden flare” and “blazing briefly” create a picture of a dramatic, bright moment, revealing how striking the detected objects are; the vivid, positive language shows admiration. D. Incorrect — the poem reveals the speaker's deep knowledge (naming objects precisely), not a simplistic understanding.

questions.question: Read lines 31-33 from the poem. The speaker refers to familiar objects and events in the lines most likely to

options.A: explain confusing information in simple terms to help the reader understand more about the topic.
options.B: demonstrate how scientific ideas can be explained by describing situations that many people are familiar with.
options.C: emphasize that the process being used to research these objects is still in the early stages of development.
options.D: suggest that the scientific language used to describe these objects seems silly by making a humorous comparison.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the speaker only gives an opinion about the names, not a simplification of confusing information about how the objects function. B. Incorrect — only describes what the names sound like, doesn't explain scientific ideas. C. Incorrect — doesn't explain the research process. D. CORRECT — “their names” (line 31) refers to scientific names (quasars, pulsars, blazars, magnetars, supernovae); the speaker opines these sound nonsensical, like villains or spells — a humorous comparison.

questions.question: Read lines 38-41 from the poem. The poet includes these lines most likely to emphasize that

options.A: it is important for astronomers to continue their research about distant signals.
options.B: these burning objects have a powerful effect on everything.
options.C: the discoveries about these objects provide little information.
options.D: the study of distant signals and the study of the moon are similar.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the lines explain the power of these objects, not the need for more research. B. CORRECT — objects that “light” everything (lines 1-4) also affect the tide in lines 38-41; the “powerful effect” keeps the tide “pulled toward the shore” while also “pointed away from” the moon — a pervasive influence. C. Incorrect — discoveries are ongoing and informative, not providing little information. D. Incorrect — the speaker is not comparing the study of distant signals with the study of the moon; the moon is just used as an example object.

questions.question: The imagery in the final stanza of the poem mainly conveys the speaker's

options.A: frustration with the limitations of astronomical research.
options.B: concern about the dangerous nature of distant signals.
options.C: interest in astronomers and their study of distant signals.
options.D: doubt about the accuracy of information gathered about distant signals.

solution.exhibit_text: A. Incorrect — the imagery conveys a positive tone (“let us notice their slow burning”), not frustration. B. Incorrect — the imagery describes a quiet, patient process, not danger. C. CORRECT — phrases like “only out there”, “write down what they can, whatever seems most real”, and “they let us notice” convey that astronomers have a rare role studying the mysteries of the universe; the speaker appreciates and is interested in their work. D. Incorrect — darkness refers to the mysteries of the universe, not secretive research processes.

sentence_paragraphs.text: In 2008, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) landed a rover, or robotic vehicle, named Horizon in the Hellas Basin region of Mars.
The rover’s mission was to search for evidence of past volcanic activity on the planet.
The rover was designed to operate on Mars for about 120 days, but Horizon’s assignment did not come to an end until nearly 11 years later in 2019.
During the rover’s mission, a high-resolution camera mounted on the rover’s robotic arm took magnified photographs of the surface of Mars.
The photographs revealed small six-sided rock formations scattered across the basin floor.
The scientists nicknamed these formations “honeycombs” based on the formations’ resemblance to a beehive.
These formations were important because their six-sided shape suggested that cooling lava may have hardened there billions of years ago.
Horizon continued to provide valuable data about ridges and other surface features.
Throughout the mission, the rover traveled a total of 19.3 miles across Mars’ surface.
When Horizon had traveled nearly the length of a half marathon, scientists celebrated the accomplishment by naming the ridge that the rover was climbing Summit Ridge.
However, in 2019, a dust storm spread all over the planet, putting the rover’s progress on hold.
Prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover.
These prevented it from charging its batteries.
Scientists then had to rely on the passing winds and dust devils to clean off the solar panels.
After the massive 2019 dust storm subsided, scientists expected to be able to reestablish communication with Horizon.
They made repeated attempts but to no avail.
In 2020, NASA finally declared Horizon’s mission complete.
Horizon was an important asset in scientists’ study of Mars; it returned valuable data about our neighbor planet and survived powerful dust storms.
NASA described the mission of Horizon as one of the most productive and long-lasting achievements in the history of planetary exploration.
Even though this rover’s journey ended, other rovers still roam the surface of Mars.

questions.question: Which sentence should follow sentence 3 to **best** introduce the topic of the passage?

options.A: Despite the challenges of operating on the surface of another planet, the Horizon rover made many valuable contributions to the field of space research.
options.B: The Horizon rover mission was a success because it revealed how lava may have once flowed across the Hellas Basin.
options.C: Throughout the historic mission of the Horizon rover, NASA scientists had to overcome challenges created by flaws in the rover’s solar panels.
options.D: The Horizon rover mission surpassed its original timeline and allowed scientists to collect additional data about the planet Mars.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the sentence that should follow sentence 3 to best introduce the topic of the passage.

A. CORRECT. This sentence best introduces the passage’s topic: Horizon made many accomplishments on its mission, despite numerous challenges. Those accomplishments include the honeycomb-formation discovery (paragraph 2), the distance traveled (paragraph 3), and the data about ridges and other surface features (paragraph 3).

B. Incorrect. Although paragraph 2 discusses how photographs taken by the rover showed formations that may have been shaped by cooling lava, this idea alone is not the topic of the entire passage.

C. Incorrect. While this sentence incorporates ideas about difficulties the scientists encountered because of dust on the rover’s solar panels (paragraph 4), the main topic of the passage is not the design flaws and obstacles scientists encountered; the passage primarily focuses on the achievements of the mission.

D. Incorrect. While it is true that the Horizon rover mission lasted much longer than planned (sentence 3), this fact is a supporting detail of the passage, not the main topic; surpassing the original timeline is only one of the rover’s many achievements mentioned in the passage.

questions.question:
Sentence 7: “These formations were important because their six-sided shape suggested that cooling lava may have hardened there billions of years ago.”

Sentence 8: “[blank] Horizon continued to provide valuable data about ridges and other surface features.”

Which word should be added to the beginning of sentence 8 to provide a better transition to the third paragraph (sentences 8–11)?

options.A: Overall,
options.B: Furthermore,
options.C: Meanwhile,
options.D: Consequently,

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the word that should be added to the beginning of sentence 8 to provide a better transition to the third paragraph (sentences 8–11).

“Overall,” is incorrect and should not be added. “Overall” would imply that all of the third paragraph features general information about Horizon, but paragraphs 2 and 3 both describe specific accomplishments (the honeycomb discovery and the distance traveled), so the transition should not move from specific to general.

“Furthermore,” is incorrect and should not be added. “Furthermore” would suggest that the author is building an argument in paragraph 2 that paragraph 3 further develops, which is not the case.

“Meanwhile,” is correct and should be added. “Meanwhile” is an appropriate transition, since the actions described in paragraph 2 (taking photographs) and paragraph 3 (traveling and gathering data) happened at the same time and both served critical functions to the overall mission.

“Consequently,” is incorrect and should not be added. “Consequently” would create a cause-and-effect relationship that does not exist between the paragraphs; the passage gives no indication that the rover’s travels resulted from the camera’s discovery.

questions.question: Which revision of sentence 11 **best** maintains the formal style established in the passage?

options.A: However, in 2019, a dust storm covered the planet, bringing the rover’s progress to a standstill.
options.B: However, in 2019, a dust storm shrouded the planet, impermanently halting the rover’s progress.
options.C: However, in 2019, a dust storm enveloped the whole of the planet, arresting the rover’s progress for a time.
options.D: However, in 2019, a dust storm covered up the whole planet, which quickly brought a stop to the progress of the rover.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the revision of sentence 11 that best maintains the formal style established in the passage.

A. CORRECT. This sentence uses clear, formal writing throughout. “Covered the planet” is accurate and formal without being overly poetic, and “standstill” is a precise word for putting something “on hold,” matching the formal style of the passage.

B. Incorrect. The word “shrouded” is overly poetic, and “impermanently halting” is too stilted for the style and tone of the passage.

C. Incorrect. The words “enveloped” and “arresting” are overly poetic, and “the whole of the planet” and “for a time” are needlessly wordy compared with the passage’s formal, scientific language.

D. Incorrect. “Covered up the whole planet” and “quickly brought a stop to the progress of the rover” are less formal and unnecessarily wordy compared with the formal style established by the rest of the passage.

questions.question:
Read this sentence.

**One of Horizon’s major contributions was discovering evidence of ancient volcanic activity on Mars.**

Where should the sentence be added to the passage?

options.A: between sentences 2 and 3
options.B: at the beginning of the second paragraph (before sentence 4)
options.C: at the end of the second paragraph (after sentence 7)
options.D: between sentences 8 and 9

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks where the sentence should be added to the passage.

A. Incorrect. Sentence 2 refers to Horizon’s mission to search for volcanic evidence, and sentence 3 mentions the rover lasting much longer than anticipated. Placing the new sentence between these two ideas, rather than at the start of the paragraph that develops it, would create a disjointed, confusing experience for the reader.

B. CORRECT. The sentence introduces the idea of discovering evidence of volcanic activity, which is the main topic of the second paragraph.

C. Incorrect. The sentence sets up the main idea of paragraph 2. As a concluding sentence, it would be repetitive and confusing.

D. Incorrect. The sentence introduces the volcanic-activity discovery, while sentences 8 and 9 discuss other surface features and the distance traveled by the rover. Adding the sentence here would create a disorganized paragraph.

questions.question: What is the **best** way to combine sentences 12 and 13?

options.A: Preventing the rover from charging its batteries, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover prior to this planet-wide dust storm.
options.B: Periodically depositing a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had prevented it from charging its batteries.
options.C: Minor dust storms, prior to this planet-wide dust storm, prevented the rover from charging its batteries because they had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover.
options.D: Prior to this planet-wide dust storm, minor dust storms had periodically deposited a layer of dust onto the solar panels of the rover, preventing it from charging its batteries.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best way to combine sentences 12 and 13.

A. Incorrect. The phrase “this planet-wide dust storm” makes a direct reference to sentence 11 and should stay at the beginning as a transition. Here it is placed at the end, making the sentence confusing and unnecessarily wordy.

B. Incorrect. This combination turns sentence 12 into an overly long dependent clause, making the connection between “it” and its antecedent, “the rover,” unclear.

C. Incorrect. This combination moves the reference to “this planet-wide dust storm” farther from sentence 11 and is unnecessarily wordy, adding “because” and repeating “the rover.”

D. CORRECT. This sentence efficiently and accurately adds sentence 13 to sentence 12 as a dependent clause by changing “These prevented” to “preventing,” while retaining the meaning of both original sentences.
